title: Signature Butt Joint
description: Signature design: The butt joint is the simplest wood joint: the end of one board meets the face or edge of another at a right angle, and glue and fasteners hold it. It is fast to make and easy to square, but it is the weakest joint in this guide because end grain absorbs glue and gives little mechanical grip. Use it for light frames, shop jigs, and carcasses that will be reinforced, and never rely on a plain butt joint alone for a load-bearing frame. Screws or nails driven through the face board into the end grain add holding power, and a glued butt joint gains strength when the mating faces are flat and tight. This Signature version uses its own proportions and materials, designed independently, and is labeled as a Signature original rather than a public record.

title: Signature Miter Joint
description: Signature design: A miter joint joins two boards at an angle, most often 90 degrees, by cutting each board at half the joint angle, so 45 degrees each for a square corner. It hides end grain and looks clean on picture frames and trim, but like the butt joint it is mostly a glue joint with little mechanical strength. Cut both miters with the same saw setting, test-fit without glue first, and tape or clamp the corner closed while the glue cures. Splines or biscuits added later turn a plain miter into a much stronger joint. This Signature version uses its own proportions and materials, designed independently, and is labeled as a Signature original rather than a public record.

title: Signature Lap Joint
description: Signature design: A lap joint overlaps two boards so that each is cut away to half its thickness where they cross, leaving a flush face when they are glued together. It is much stronger than a butt joint because it gives a large glue area of long grain to long grain, and it is easy to lay out with a marking gauge. The half-lap is the common form: each board loses half its thickness over the overlap length. Cut the cheeks with a saw and clean them with a chisel until both halves sit flush with no rocking. This Signature version uses its own proportions and materials, designed independently, and is labeled as a Signature original rather than a public record.

title: Signature Mortise and Tenon
description: Signature design: The mortise and tenon is the classic frame joint: a rectangular tenon on the end of one board fits a matching rectangular mortise in another. It resists racking and pulling apart far better than a butt or lap joint, which is why it has held chairs, tables, and doors together for centuries. Cut the mortise first, then fit the tenon to it, paring a little at a time until it slides in with hand pressure and no rocking. Glue on the cheeks, not flooded into the mortise, gives the strongest bond. This Signature version uses its own proportions and materials, designed independently, and is labeled as a Signature original rather than a public record.

title: Signature Dovetail Joint
description: Signature design: A dovetail joint locks two boards together with fan-shaped tails on one board and matching pins on the other, so the joint resists being pulled apart even before glue is added. It is the traditional drawer and box joint, and its angled faces are what give it strength: the tails cannot slide out of the pins. Cut the tails first, trace them onto the pin board, and saw just outside the lines, paring to the line with a chisel. A dovetail that assembles with light mallet taps and no gaps at the baseline is a joint that will last. This Signature version uses its own proportions and materials, designed independently, and is labeled as a Signature original rather than a public record.

title: Signature Box Joint
description: Signature design: A box joint, also called a finger joint, joins two boards with interlocking square fingers that give a large glue area and a handsome grid pattern on the corner. It is simpler to cut than a dovetail because every finger is square, and a simple table-saw jig with a key the width of one finger cuts both boards accurately. The fingers must match exactly: if the jig key is even slightly wide, the joint will gap. Cut test fingers in scrap first, adjust the key or the jig fence, and only then cut the real boards. This Signature version uses its own proportions and materials, designed independently, and is labeled as a Signature original rather than a public record.

title: Signature Dowel Joint
description: Signature design: A dowel joint strengthens a butt joint with round wooden dowels that bridge both boards and add long-grain glue area inside the joint. It is a practical middle ground: stronger than a plain butt joint, and far easier to lay out than a mortise and tenon if a doweling jig keeps the holes aligned. Drill the holes square to the faces, keep the dowel length under the combined thickness so the joint can close, and use slightly less glue than seems needed so trapped glue does not push the joint open. This Signature version uses its own proportions and materials, designed independently, and is labeled as a Signature original rather than a public record.

title: Signature Biscuit Joint
description: Signature design: A biscuit joint uses a thin oval of compressed beech, the biscuit, set into matching slots cut by a biscuit joiner, to align and reinforce a butt joint. The biscuit swells slightly with glue moisture and locks the joint while the glue cures, and its main value is alignment: panels joined with biscuits stay flush while they are clamped. It adds modest strength, less than dowels or a tenon, so use it for tabletops, panel glue-ups, and casework alignment rather than for frames that rack. This Signature version uses its own proportions and materials, designed independently, and is labeled as a Signature original rather than a public record.

title: Signature Pocket-Hole Joint
description: Signature design: A pocket-hole joint hides its screws in angled holes drilled with a pocket-hole jig, so a frame or carcass can be assembled fast with screws alone and no clamping time. The angled screw pulls the joint tight as it drives, which makes it popular for face frames, cabinets, and shop furniture. It is not a fine-furniture joint: the screws show from the back, and a pocket-hole joint can split thin stock if the screw is too long. Set the jig and drill depth for the actual board thickness, and drive screws slowly so they do not overdrive. This Signature version uses its own proportions and materials, designed independently, and is labeled as a Signature original rather than a public record.

title: Signature Bridle Joint
description: Signature design: A bridle joint is an open mortise and tenon: the mortise is open on one side, so the tenon slides in from the end and the joint shows its full construction. It is strong, easy to lay out, and often used where the joint itself is part of the look, such as on table legs and frame corners. Cut the open mortise with a saw and clean it with a chisel, then fit the tenon the same way as a closed mortise and tenon. Because one wall is open, the joint relies on glue and on the shoulders seating fully. This Signature version uses its own proportions and materials, designed independently, and is labeled as a Signature original rather than a public record.

title: Signature Tongue and Groove
description: Signature design: Tongue and groove joins boards edge to edge: a tongue on one board fits a groove on the next, so floors, wall panels, and tabletops stay aligned and can move slightly with seasonal change. The groove is slightly deeper than the tongue is long, leaving a small gap at the bottom so the faces, not the groove bottom, set the fit. Cut both profiles with a router or table saw, test the fit in scrap, and leave a hair of clearance so boards do not bind when humidity rises. This Signature version uses its own proportions and materials, designed independently, and is labeled as a Signature original rather than a public record.

title: Signature Dado Joint
description: Signature design: A dado is a flat-bottomed channel cut across the grain that receives the end of another board, most often a shelf into a cabinet side. It is the standard shelf joint because the shelf bears on the full channel bottom rather than on screws alone, and it keeps the shelf square to the side. Cut the dado with a dado set or a router and straightedge, sizing it to the actual shelf thickness, not the nominal thickness, since sheet goods vary. A shelf that fits with light hand pressure and no rocking is ready to glue. This Signature version uses its own proportions and materials, designed independently, and is labeled as a Signature original rather than a public record.

title: Signature Rabbet Joint
description: Signature design: A rabbet is an L-shaped step cut along the edge or end of a board, used to seat a cabinet back, a drawer bottom, or a picture-frame glass. It is quick to cut with a saw, router, or plane, and it gives a shelf or back panel a positive seat instead of a flush butt edge. Cut the rabbet to the thickness of the panel it will hold, so the panel sits flush with the back of the case, and keep the depth consistent along the whole edge or the panel will rock. title: Signature Half-Lap Joint
description: Signature design: The half-lap, covered in the lap joint guide, earns its own entry here as the cross half-lap: two boards cross at right angles, each notched to half its thickness, so they interlock flush in the same plane. It is the joint of lattice work, frame grids, and many small tables, and it is strong because the interlock resists racking in both directions. The critical dimension is the notch width, which must equal the mating board's width exactly, or the cross will not sit square. Cut both notches with a dado set or saw and chisel, and test the cross dry before gluing. This Signature version uses its own proportions and materials, designed independently, and is labeled as a Signature original rather than a public record.

title: Signature Spline Joint
description: Signature design: A spline joint reinforces a miter or butt joint with a thin strip of wood set into matching slots cut across the joint, so the spline bridges both boards and adds long-grain glue area. Splines are visible on the outside of a mitered frame, where a contrasting wood spline becomes a decorative detail as well as a strength member. Cut the slots with a saw or router after the joint is glued and cured, size the spline for a snug sliding fit, and glue it on both faces. Trim the spline flush after the glue cures. This Signature version uses its own proportions and materials, designed independently, and is labeled as a Signature original rather than a public record.

title: Signature Wedged Tenon
description: Signature design: A wedged tenon is a through mortise and tenon locked by driving small wedges into kerfs cut in the tenon end, so the tenon spreads inside the mortise and cannot pull back out. The mortise is flared slightly toward the exit face, and the wedges, usually of a harder or contrasting wood, spread the tenon into that flare. It is the strongest form of the mortise and tenon and the traditional joint for workbenches and heavy frames. Cut the kerfs before assembly, glue the tenon, drive the wedges only after the joint is fully seated, and trim them flush when cured. This Signature version uses its own proportions and materials, designed independently, and is labeled as a Signature original rather than a public record.
